tagline: Deliver the rumors. Dodge the drama. Pick up Bomba. An original arcade game: Federico drives a site cart along an angled jobsite route throwing gossip at the crews, dodging eighteen kinds of obstacle, while the rumor mutates on its way to Bomba at the trailer office.

pieces.name: Foundation + projection
pieces.note: 60Hz fixed-step loop, action-named input with edge detection, seeded RNG, road-space projection with per-row surface scan, sprite + footprint registry, capture harness, procedural soundtrack.

pieces.name: Art
pieces.note: Rebuilt at 384x288 against the concept sheet: the cream site cart with Federico silhouetted against a shadowed cab, an outlined crew base with palette-swapped hats and vests, Bomba as a person, the superintendent, all six scaffold materials, the heavy equipment, five power ups, and a trailer office drawn rather than stamped.

pieces.name: Buggy feel + throwing
pieces.note: Speed-scaled steering authority, roll-on throttle, off-road drag, crash and recover with invulnerability, two-sided throwing plus a nearest-target assist, sheets on a real ballistic arc.

pieces.name: Hazards + targets
pieces.note: The sheet's own eighteen: scaffold material, crew who stand in front of it, and machines that do not look where they are going — each with the line the site shouts at you.

pieces.name: Levels 1-8 + spawner
pieces.note: Eight themed shifts, deterministic route generation from a seed, escalating hazard mix and speed caps, the rumour chain threaded through all of them.

pieces.name: Score, upgrades, Bomba payoff
pieces.note: Quality x combo scoring, near misses, the five named power ups, nine upgrades, HUD with live fuel timers, and the trailer-office payoff where Bomba hands back a fresh rumour.

pieces.name: Progress page + regression
pieces.note: Static server, screenshot tour, this page, a browser-free verifier over the shipped data, an autopilot that plays all eight shifts, and CI running the lot on every push.

loops.note: projection proven by capture before anything was built on it
throw path found broken by the first capture and fixed
target placement retuned against measured throw range
autopilot clears every shift end to end
verifier asserts route fairness and throw geometry without a browser, in 0.14s
playtest now takes the most disruptive upgrade on offer, which is how HIGH LOB was caught

findings.title: The hero sprite was a cream blob for three iterations
findings.detail: Federico's cart was drawn in the same cream as its own roof, so the driver was invisible and the whole vehicle read as a box. Gameplay screenshots are far too small to diagnose a 22px sprite, so this survived several passes. Fixed by building tools/artsheet.mjs, which renders every sprite at 4x on a checkerboard: the problem was obvious in one look, and the fix — a shadowed cab for Federico to silhouette against, plus heavy outlines on the whole cast the way the concept sheet has them — took minutes once it could be seen.

findings.title: A rolling pipe could wall off the road on its own
findings.detail: The wind-blown pipe was given a 3.6m footprint on an 11m road, so a single one near the centre left 2.77m of clean surface against a 2.8m minimum — not threadable by a 2m cart. The route verifier caught it on one seed in sixty-four. Narrowed to 3.0m and biased away from the centre line.

findings.title: Nobody could throw anything
findings.detail: The throw gate tested `buggy.cooldown <= 0`, but the field was never initialised, so the comparison was `undefined <= 0` — false forever. Every throw in the game was silently swallowed. The first capture tour caught it: sheets never appeared and the delivery counter stayed on zero through a full route.

findings.title: Crews stood outside throwing range
findings.detail: Targets were placed 10.1-12.1 m off the centre line against a base throw range of 8 m, so most deliveries were geometrically impossible even with the buggy hugging the kerb. Crews moved in to 9.3-10.9 m and the base range went to 10 m, which makes the near side comfortable and the far side a decision.

findings.title: Every delivery scored as a whisper
findings.detail: Hit quality was measured where the sheet happened to be on the frame contact was detected — which is always the edge of the hitbox — so the autopilot landed 15 deliveries in a row and every one of them graded as the worst tier. Quality now comes from the throw's closest approach to the crew, solved from the sheet's velocity. Bullseyes went from 0 per shift to 11.

findings.title: Scaffold crews were unreachable
findings.detail: Crews on scaffolds had a hitbox starting 2.4 m up while a sheet's arc peaked at 1.76 m. Every scaffold delivery from level 5 onward was geometrically impossible. The arc now peaks at 2.09 m and the scaffold hitbox starts at 1.6 m, so reaching one means getting closer than you would for a crew on the ground — a real distinction instead of an impossible one.

findings.title: Some generated routes could not be driven
findings.detail: Route generation could place solid hazards across the full paved width with no gap to thread, and could bury a crew's approach behind them. On one seed the autopilot failed the same shift three times with eight crashes a run, while another seed of the same shift cleared 20 of 20. Generation now runs a fairness pass: hazards that would leave less than 2.8 m of clean surface are dropped, and the outer half of a crew's own side is cleared for the 13 m run-up.

findings.title: Shipped unplayable on a phone
findings.detail: Input was keyboard-only, so a touchscreen had literally no way to steer or throw, and the canvas floored its scale to an integer with a minimum of 1x, leaving a 288px picture adrift on a 390px phone. Neither the capture tour nor the autopilot could see it: both drove the game through synthetic key events at a desktop viewport. Reported by the player, not the harness. Fixed with on-screen controls mapped onto the same named actions the keyboard uses, fractional scaling below 2x, a handheld layout in portrait and letterbox-floating controls in landscape. The capture tour now has a --mobile mode that runs at a phone viewport with touch enabled and asserts the controls appear, the picture fills the width, the steer button moves the buggy and the throw button costs a sheet.

findings.title: One upgrade quietly broke the whole game
findings.detail: HIGH LOB raises the throw arc, and a raised arc sails clean over a crew whose catch window has a low ceiling. Taking it meant every ground delivery for the rest of the run passed above every crew's head: the autopilot threw 19 sheets on a shift and landed none of them. Because upgrade offers are random, it only reproduced in some sessions. Ground crews now have a catch window tall enough to take a lob, HIGH LOB is capped at one copy, and the playtest deliberately takes the most disruptive upgrade on offer rather than whatever the cursor was on.

findings.title: The fairness pass had a hole it could not see
findings.detail: The first version of the drivable-line pass checked each hazard only against those already placed behind it, so a hazard that was fine against its predecessors and fine against its successors could still be lethal with both at once. The verifier asserts the property from both directions and found 13 walled-off routes across 64 seeds. Generation now repairs until the property actually holds, dropping whichever member of the tightest wall opens it up most.

findings.title: Combos could not chain
findings.detail: The combo held for 2.6 s while crews sit about three seconds apart at cruise, so the meter reset between every delivery and never passed x2. Raised to 4.2 s: a clean shift now runs to x14.

findings.title: The road would have rendered as a staircase
findings.detail: Drawing the surface as one axis-aligned rect per metre stairsteps the diagonal edges. The projection is instead inverted per screen row, so the road centre on row y is a closed form and the edges land on exact positions. Designed in from the start and documented in road.js rather than discovered late.

galleries.title: Every sprite, magnified
galleries.note: The contact sheet from tools/artsheet.mjs — the whole ART table at 4x on a checkerboard. This is the tool that made the art iterable; before it existed, sprite defects were invisible at gameplay scale.

galleries.title: The standard tour
galleries.note: Every screen the game has, captured from the real running build by tools/shoot.mjs: attract loop, brief, the route, a crash, results, the stores, and the payoff at the far gate.

galleries.title: On a phone
galleries.note: A 390x844 viewport with touch actually enabled, driven through the on-screen controls. Portrait stacks the picture over a control deck; landscape floats the buttons onto the letterbox bars. Every shot here is backed by an assertion that the touch did something.

timeline.label: Foundation and projection
timeline.detail: 60Hz engine, input remapped for driving and two-sided throwing, and 288x216 because a 4:3 screen gives an angled route the vertical room it needs to telegraph hazards.

timeline.label: Contracts pinned
timeline.detail: CONTRACTS.md fixed ownership, the feel targets a critic can measure, and the humour rules. art/names.js pins every sprite name AND its road-space hitbox, so gameplay and art can never disagree about how big a thing is.

timeline.label: Whole game built and captured
timeline.detail: Art, driving, hazards and targets, the eight routes, and the scoring and payoff, each verified against the real running game rather than against intent.

timeline.label: Autopilot regression
timeline.detail: tools/bot.js drives every shift to the far gate. It caught the throw range mismatch immediately and now guards against any tuning change that makes a shift unclearable.

timeline.label: Repo assembled
timeline.detail: A browser-free verifier over the shipped data, CI running verify + playtest + capture on every push, and a Pages workflow so the play link is real. The verifier immediately found a hole in the route fairness pass and, once pointed at throw geometry, the upgrade that broke every ground delivery.

timeline.label: Rebuilt around the concept sheet
timeline.detail: The player sent the design sheet the game was supposed to be, and it showed real drift: Bomba was a person, not a dog; the shift ended at a trailer office, not a fence; Federico drove a cream cart. Resolution went to 384x288 because an 8px worker cannot carry a hard hat, a vest and a face. The catalogue, the power ups, the chaos tier and the ending were rebuilt to match.
